result.summary: Orpheus, sitting among the trees and beasts his music has drawn, begins a song invoking Jove and announces a lighter theme: youths loved by the gods. His first tale is of Jupiter, who becomes an eagle and carries off Ganymede to serve as cup-bearer.

scenes.title: Orpheus begins his song
scenes.summary: Orpheus, surrounded by trees, beasts and birds, tunes his lyre and invokes the Muse and Jove. He says he will now sing a softer theme of youths loved by gods.

place.name: the grove of trees drawn by Orpheus

scenes.title: Jupiter carries off Ganymede
scenes.summary: Jupiter, desiring Ganymede, takes the form of an eagle, the bird that carries his bolts, and seizes the Trojan youth. Ganymede now serves nectar to Jove, against Juno's wishes.
scenes.stakes: Ganymede is snatched from his home; Jupiter risks Juno's displeasure.

alias_notes.explanation: Jove is another name for Jupiter.
Orpheus addresses his mother, the Muse; the text does not name her here, but tradition says Calliope.

notable_quotes.reason: Orpheus' invocation, 'all things submit to the sway of Jove', opens his song.

analysis.text: Orpheus turns from epic subjects to love stories of gods and mortals, framing the book's run of tales about forbidden or punished desire.
The Ganymede myth reflected Greek and Roman traditions of male desire and the elite cup-bearer, which Ovid presents with court-like elegance.

legacy.text: The rape of Ganymede became a frequent subject in art, including Correggio's painting (c. 1530) and Rembrandt's 1635 version.

fun_facts.text: The word 'nectar' in the passage is the gods' drink, and Ganymede's role as cup-bearer replaced Hebe's in some traditions.

language_notes.text: The poet tests the lyre's strings, finding that different notes still blend in harmony, before beginning his song.
The Muse is called "parent" because Calliope, Muse of epic poetry, was said to be Orpheus's mother.
The Giants warred against the gods; Jove defeated them with thunderbolts at Phlegræa (Phlegra) in Thessaly or Macedonia.
Jupiter preferred to be something other than himself: an eagle, so that he could seize the boy.
"Vouchsafe" means to condescend or deign to do something.
"Ilium" is Troy; Ganymede is a Trojan prince.

context_notes.text: Orpheus has just drawn trees and animals by his music; the grove of trees gathered around him provides shade.
Juno, Jove's wife, resented Ganymede because he replaced her daughter Hebe as the gods' cup-bearer.

literary_notes.text: Orpheus opens by calling on the Muse and Jove, following the epic convention of beginning a song with divine inspiration.
The announced theme of forbidden loves and punished girls prepares for the tales that follow, such as Myrrha and Venus.
The ruler of all gods is described as wishing to be something lesser, a bird, which wittily shows his power ruled by desire.
"Fictitious wings" stresses that the eagle form is a disguise, since Jove is a god, not a bird.
